SQL debugging practice: fix the query an AI wrote

12 practice questions that start from a query instead of a blank editor. An AI assistant wrote each one for the task. It runs, it returns a believable answer, and the answer is wrong. Find the line, fix the query, and the checker grades your fix against the expected result.

Reviewing a query you did not write is part of the job: a colleague’s, an old dashboard’s, or one an assistant drafted in a second. The bugs that matter raise no error, so this set trains the habit that catches them: check what the query returns, not how it reads.

Fix your first query

How it works: spot, fix, learn

  1. Spot. Read the task and the AI’s query, and tap the line you think is wrong. This step is optional and scored on its own.
  2. Fix. Edit the query and submit it. Run the original first if you like, and compare its rows with the expected ones to see what the bug does.
  3. Learn. After a correct fix, one line says what the bug was, with a link to the trap page when there is one.

The bugs in the set

  • A date bound that drops the last dayBETWEEN '…-01' AND '…-07' on a timestamp column stops at midnight on the 7th, so every row later that day is lost. Read the trap
  • GROUP BY on the wrong columnsGroup by too few columns and different rows are averaged together; group by a raw timestamp and every row becomes its own group.
  • Integer divisionAn integer divided by an integer stays an integer in SQLite, so a rate loses its decimals before ROUND ever sees them.
  • COUNT(*) against COUNT(column)COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) and AVG(column) skip NULLs, so a count next to an average can describe different rows.
  • NOT IN with a NULL in the listOne NULL in the subquery makes every NOT IN comparison unknown, and the query quietly returns nothing. Read the trap
  • A WHERE that undoes a LEFT JOINA filter on the right-hand table in WHERE throws away the unmatched rows the LEFT JOIN was there to keep. Read the trap
  • Ties in a rankingROW_NUMBER never ties; RANK and DENSE_RANK do. Pick the one the question’s tie rule describes.
  • DISTINCT in the wrong placeDISTINCT inside an aggregate collapses equal values, so repeated quantities are counted once instead of every time.
  • JOIN fan-outJoin one parent to two child tables and every pair repeats, so both totals are multiplied. Read the trap
  • An average of averagesAveraging per-group averages weighs a group of two the same as a group of two hundred. Read the trap
  • The wrong window partitionA running total partitioned by the wrong column restarts at the wrong place and mixes rows that do not belong together.

Why a GROUP BY runs in SQLite and fails in PostgreSQL

Runs in SQLite, refused by PostgreSQL

SELECT category,
       product,
       ROUND(SUM(total), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY category;

In SQLite this runs and returns two rows, one per category. Each row shows the whole category’s revenue (4,984.68 for Electronics) next to one product name SQLite took from one of the category’s rows. Electronics has 23 products, and the row reads as if that one product earned all of it. Laptop Pro, the top seller, brought in 1,299.99.

PostgreSQL refuses the same query with an error that orders.product must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function, and MySQL’s default mode refuses it too. SQLite is the lenient one: a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated gets a value from some row of the group. The error is the database asking you what you meant. Answer it one of two ways. (In PostgreSQL, ROUND(x, 2) takes a NUMERIC: if total is a float column, write ROUND(SUM(total)::numeric, 2), or PostgreSQL stops at the ROUND before it reaches the GROUP BY.)

Fix 1: You wanted revenue per product: group by every column you show

SELECT category,
       product,
       ROUND(SUM(total), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY category, product
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;
categoryproductrevenue
ElectronicsLaptop Pro1,299.99
FurnitureStanding Desk599.99
ElectronicsGraphics Card549.99

Fix 2: You wanted revenue per category: put the product inside an aggregate

SELECT category,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS products,
       ROUND(SUM(total), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;
categoryproductsrevenue
Electronics234,984.68
Furniture173,171.76

Rule of thumb. Every column in the SELECT list is either in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. If SQLite accepted a query that breaks this rule, the number is not wrong yet, but the label next to it can be.

Questions

What is a SQL debugging exercise?

A task, a dataset and a query that already runs but returns the wrong answer. You find the line that is wrong, fix the query, and submit it. The fix is graded like any SQL Quest challenge: your result is compared with the expected rows.

Did an AI assistant really write these queries?

Each query is presented as an AI assistant’s draft, because that is the situation you meet when you review one. We wrote and checked every query ourselves, so each has one known defect and an expected result to grade your fix against.

Do I have to find the wrong line before I fix it?

No. Tapping the line you think is wrong is optional and scored on its own, as your spot accuracy. It never blocks the fix and a wrong tap never costs you a solve.

Which SQL dialect do the questions use?

SQLite, running in your browser. The bugs in this set are about logic, not dialect: the same JOIN, NULL, date and window mistakes return wrong answers in PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery or Snowflake.

Why does my GROUP BY query run in SQLite but fail in PostgreSQL?

SQLite lets you select a column that is neither in the GROUP BY nor inside an aggregate, and fills it with a value from some row of the group. PostgreSQL and MySQL’s default mode refuse that query. Either add the column to the GROUP BY, if you wanted one row per value of it, or wrap it in an aggregate such as COUNT(DISTINCT …) or MAX(…), if you wanted one row per group. The worked example on this page shows both on the same data.
